---
title: "Floral polymorphisms"
---

## Fire-driven diversity
<div class="research-section">
  <div class="research-text">

Fire is a common disturbance in the Fynbos, as in all mediterranean ecosytstems.
This creates both temporal and spatial heterogeneity, which can promote diversity.

Some populations of *Lapeirousia anceps* are bimodal in tube length, 
i.e. both short- and long-tubed plants coexist. Early after a fire, their 
long-tongued fly pollinators visit the flowers more frequently. At the same time, 
long-tubed plants are more abundant and produce more seeds 
than short-tubed plants. However, after a few years, the flies become rare and 
short-tubed plants, which can self-pollinate more easily, flower more frequently 
and produce more seeds than long-tubed plants. Thus, selection favours the two 
forms during different stages of post-fire succession and thereby contributes to 
their co-existence. 

  </div>

## Variation in anther morphology
<div class="research-section">
  <div class="research-text">
  
Anther structure is one of the most important determinants of pollen transfer. 
In *Cyanella alba* populations differ in anther dehiscense, with some having 
poricidal anthers, and others dehiscing laterally. Poricidal anthers are usually 
indicative of buzz-pollination, but *C. alba* flowers with poricidal anthers receive 
no visits from buzzing insects, export little pollen and produce few seeds. 
On the other hand, populations with laterally 
dehiscing anthers lose more pollen to the environment, but they can also utilize 
the numerous non-buzzing flower visitors as pollinators. 

  </div>
